The East Hollow committee's September 2019 memorandum, signed by Rina Vale, describes a token scheme during repairs to the district footbridge. Thirty households appear on its register, ten from each of three lanes. The token permits a household to use the staffed service crossing during its assigned morning window. A clerk puts a triangular mark on a token at issue. At the service crossing, the attendant adds a short horizontal stroke after admitting the household. These marks document different events. A triangle is not evidence that anyone actually crossed. Tokens carry a lane identifier and issue date; a steward checks both before admitting a group.

If the service crossing closes before a household's window ends, its token can be moved to the following morning once. The clerk must first confirm the closure with the attendant. The document does not allow a household to hand its token to another household. Goods carried by the admitted group receive no separate priority.

For a retrospective check, the committee selected twelve issued tokens. Nine had corresponding entries in the crossing ledger; three did not. The memorandum leaves both unused tokens and incomplete ledger pages as possible explanations for the unmatched cases. It reports no investigation of individual households and assigns no penalty for an unmatched entry alone.

A worked example describes a household arriving in the afternoon instead of its morning window. It joins the ordinary queue; the attendant does not erase and replace the token's window. This example explains how the recorded scheduling rule was applied, rather than prescribing a response to every possible emergency. The author concludes that the marks can distinguish issue from admission when both records survive. The check cannot establish how often people crossed without a token or whether the arrangement shortened average waiting times.

Four unmatched records, rather than a claim of misconduct, are the puzzle in Mira Doren's account of the West Orchard crossing arrangements. Her note is dated November 2021. Staff compared fifteen temporary tokens with admission sheets, finding a corresponding entry for eleven. A token might have remained unused, or its admission sheet might have gone missing. The note does not settle which explanation applies to any of the four cases.

The arrangement began while a damaged hillside footbridge was closed. Twenty-four registered households, organized in three groups of eight, could use a supervised service crossing. Each token identified the group and the afternoon period allocated to it. Its purpose was access scheduling, not ownership of a crossing place. It conveyed no authority to use the damaged bridge.

Reading a token requires distinguishing two inscriptions: the office's circular issue stamp and the attendant's vertical admission line. Only the second records that the group was admitted. A circular stamp by itself cannot establish a crossing. The office recorded an issue day alongside the group identifier.

An afternoon closure could justify a single extension to the next afternoon, but only after the attendant confirmed that service had stopped. Holders could not pass the permission to another household. The same token also gave no special entitlement for carried goods. In a described late-arrival case, a family appeared the following morning and was placed in the ordinary queue instead of having its afternoon allocation rewritten.

Doren cautions against using the small check to calculate total unauthorized crossings. The staff made no household-by-household inquiry, and unmatched paperwork alone incurred no sanction. Surviving pairs of records can show a distinction between issuance and admission; they do not demonstrate a reduction in waiting time or the completeness of every day's sheets.
